Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 1:

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque⟩

Tafsir of Surat Bani Isra'il

It is Meccan, except for five verses, which we will mention in their places.

It is narrated from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "Surat Bani Isra'il, al-Kahf, Maryam and Ta-Ha are among my old possessions (talad), and they are among the first of the 'atiq (the earliest revealed)."

God the Exalted says: ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night⟩. Subhan (glorification, transcendence): the declaration of God's freedom from every imperfection. Its real meaning is the magnification of God through the form of intensification (al-mubalagha), and the attribution to Him of freedom from every deficiency.

The word subhan is a defective word (kalima mumtani'a) that is not permitted to be applied to anyone other than God, because intensive magnification is not fitting for anyone other than God. It does not inflect in the way many verbal nouns (masadir) do. Since it cannot be applied to anyone other than God, and its forms do not vary, it likewise follows a single pattern in inflection (sarf).

As for tasbih (glorification) in the Qur'an, it occurs in several senses. It has come with the meaning of prayer (salat), God the Exalted says: ﴿Had he not been among those who glorify [God]⟩, i.e., among those who pray.

It has come with the meaning of exception (istithna'), God the Exalted says: ﴿The best of them said: Did I not tell you, "Why do you not glorify [God]?"⟩, i.e., "Why do you not make the exception (tastathnuna)?"

It has come with the meaning of transcendence (tanzih), which is God the Exalted's saying: ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night⟩. It has come in a report with the meaning of light, as in the report in which he said: "Had He removed the veils (subuhat) of His face, the glances of His sight would have been burned away by what they reached," i.e., the light of His face. It is also reported on the authority of the Prophet that he explained "Subhan Allah" as "the declaration of God's freedom from every evil."

The phrase ﴿took His servant⟩ (asra bi-'abdihi) means: he made him travel by night, and likewise sara bihi. The poet said:

(And a night full of dew I traveled, and the one who would have turned me back from its journey was not blamed...)

The phrase ﴿His servant⟩ means Muhammad. It has been narrated from the Prophet that he said: "God took me as a servant before He took me as a messenger."

The phrase ﴿by night⟩ is mentioned to indicate that it was during part of the night.

Ibn Mas'ud recited: "asra bi-'abdihi min al-layl (took His servant by night)." The phrase ﴿from the Sacred Mosque⟩: scholars differ regarding the place from which the Messenger of God was taken on the journey. One opinion is that it was from the Sacred Mosque, and the apparent meaning of the verse indicates this.

It is reported from Muhammad ibn Ali al-Baqir that the Prophet said: "I was sleeping in al-Hijr, when Jibril (peace be upon him) came to me and moved me gently, and said: 'O Muhammad, rise, to go forth to your Lord.'"

The second opinion is that he was taken from the house of Umm Hani' bint Abi Talib, and this is in the narration of Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.

Opinions differ regarding the time of the journey. Muqatil said it was one year before the Hijra. It is said that it was in Rajab, and it is said in Ramadan. Some said he was taken when he was fifty-one years, nine months, and twenty-eight days old, and God knows best.

The phrase ﴿to the Farthest Mosque⟩ means the Mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), and it was named the Farthest (al-Aqsa) because of its distance from the Sacred Mosque.

The phrase ﴿whose surroundings We have blessed⟩ means with water and trees. It has also been said: "We blessed its surroundings" because it is the place of the prophets and the descent-place of the angels.

The phrase ﴿That We might show him some of Our signs⟩ means some of the wonders of Our power. He saw the prophets there, and he saw their traces.

The phrase ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing⟩: the mention of "All-Hearing" here indicates that He answers his supplication, and the mention of "All-Seeing" indicates that He was the Guardian over him in the darkness of the night.

As for the discussion of the Night Journey (al-isra'), opinions differ on whether he was taken with his body and soul or with his soul alone. The majority hold that he was taken with both body and soul together. It is reported from Aisha, may God be pleased with her, that she said: "The body of the Messenger of God was not lost; rather he was taken by night in his soul alone."

Sound reports have been transmitted in unbroken succession (tawatarat) in agreement with the first opinion, and the most complete of them is the hadith of Anas from Malik ibn Sa'sa'a, from the Prophet, in which he was taken to Bayt al-Maqdis, and from there to the heaven, and Jibril asked the lowest heaven to open. It was said to him: "Who is with you?" He said: "Muhammad, peace be upon him."

They said: "Has he been sent?" He said: "Yes."

They said: "Welcome to him; what a fine visit this is!" The same occurred in every heaven. It is also mentioned in it that in the lowest heaven he saw Adam, peace be upon him; in the second heaven, the two maternal cousins, Isa and Yahya; in the third heaven, Yusuf; in the fourth heaven, Idris, peace be upon him; in the fifth heaven, Harun; in the sixth heaven, Musa; in the seventh heaven, Ibrahim. In it he said: "I was raised to the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary (Sidrat al-Muntaha); its leaves were like the ears of elephants, and its fruits like the jars of Hajar. I saw four rivers issuing from its base: two hidden rivers and two apparent rivers. As for the hidden ones, they are in Paradise; as for the apparent ones, they are the Nile and the Euphrates." It is also mentioned in it that God the Exalted made fifty prayers obligatory upon him... the story at length, until they were reduced to five.

A group of Companions narrated accounts similar to this story, among them Ibn Abbas, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman, Abu Hurayra, and others.

Ma'mar narrated from Qatada, from Anas, from the Prophet, that Jibril (peace be upon him) brought al-Buraq, saddled and bridled, and the Messenger wanted to mount it, but it was restive with him. Jibril said to it: "By God, no one has ever ridden you who is more honoured before God than he," and it sweated profusely. Abu Isa mentioned this in his Jami'.

It is firmly established from the Prophet that he said: "I was brought a beast smaller than a mule and larger than a donkey, whose stride reached as far as its gaze could reach." It is also firmly established from the Prophet that he said: "I saw Musa on the night I was taken by night; he was like one of the men of Shanu'a. I saw Isa, of medium height and reddish, as if he had come out of a bathhouse. And I saw Ibrahim; your companion is the most similar of people to him."

In this report he also said: "I was brought two vessels, one containing milk and the other wine. I took the milk and drank it. Jibril said: 'You have chosen the natural disposition (al-fitra). As for you, had you taken the wine, your community would have gone astray.'"

In the story: when he rose in the morning, people spoke of his journey, and many people were tempted, and a group of those who had believed in him and affirmed him apostatized. The polytheists came to Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, and said to him: "Do you not see your companion claiming that he was taken to Bayt al-Maqdis and returned in the same night, while we travel for a month on the backs of camels to reach it!" Abu Bakr said: "If he said that, then he has spoken the truth." They said: "Do you believe such a thing?" He said: "Yes, and more than that; I believe him that news of heaven comes to him in the morning or evening."

It is firmly established from the Prophet that he said: "I was standing in al-Hijr, and Bayt al-Maqdis was raised up for me, so I began describing it to them." This was when they asked him about its description.

In the story: the polytheists asked him about a caravan of theirs on the road, and he said: "It has reached such-and-such a place, and leading it is a grey camel." They said: "And when will it arrive?" He said: "At sunrise." So some of them went out watching for the caravan, and some watched for the sunrise. Those said: "This caravan has come," and these said: "The sun has risen."

It is also narrated that he said: "I passed by a covered vessel full of water; I drank some of it and left the rest." The caravan was asked about that, and they reported its form.

"The saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿And We gave Moses the Book﴾ — the verse. He means: We gave Moses the Book, and it is the Torah.

And His saying: ﴿And We made it a guidance for the Children of Israel﴾ — meaning: the Children of Israel are guided by it. And His saying: ﴿that you not take﴾ is read in two ways: with the ta' (tu-) and with the ya' (yu-). Whoever reads it with the ta', its meaning is: "And We gave Moses the Book, commanding you, 'Do not take'…" And whoever reads it with the ya', its meaning is: "And We made a covenant with them that they should not take…" His saying: ﴿a guardian other than Me﴾ — meaning: a partner. It has also been said that its meaning is: We commanded them not to rely upon other than Me, and not to take lords besides Me."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 3:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The offspring of those whom We carried with Noah﴾. Its meaning: O offspring of those whom We carried with Noah. Mujahid read it with a fatha on the dhal (dhurriyyata). And it is related from Zayd ibn Thabit, in some narrations: "dhurriyyati man hamalna ma'a Nuh," with a kasra on the dhal. He only said ﴿The offspring of those whom We carried with Noah﴾ because the creation now are the descendants of Noah, as we explained earlier.

And His saying: ﴿whom We carried﴾ means: in the ship.

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, he was a grateful servant﴾. He was named Noah (Nuh) because of his frequent lamenting (nawh) over himself. It was also said: his name was Abd al-Ghaffar. This was mentioned by al-Naqqash in his tafsir.

As for his gratitude: it is narrated that when he ate he would say, "Praise be to God," and when he drank he would say, "Praise be to God," and when he dressed he would say, "Praise be to God." In some narrations: when he entered he would say, "Praise be to God," and when he left he would say, "Praise be to God," and likewise in standing and sitting.

It is also narrated that he did not take a single step without mentioning God Exalted, so He said: ﴿Indeed, he was a grateful servant﴾, meaning: one who gives abundant thanks.

The Words of the Exalted: ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Scripture﴾, and so on. Al-qada' (decree): the separating of a matter through rulings. The meaning of "qadayna" here is: We revealed to them and informed them.

It has also been said that its meaning is: And We decreed upon the Children of Israel in the Scripture.

As for His words: ﴿You will surely cause corruption on the earth twice﴾, meaning: you will surely disobey on the earth twice. And His words: ﴿and you will surely become haughty﴾, meaning: you will surely magnify yourselves, transgress, and act arrogantly.

As for His words: ﴿with a great exaltation﴾, meaning: a great pride, immense.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 5:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So when the promise of the first of them came﴾ means: the first of the two times. In the narrative it is reported that their corruption in the first instance was by killing the Prophet Isaiah (Ishaya) – peace be upon him – and by their committing sins and rejecting what they had been commanded. Some exegeses report that they worshipped idols.

The land mentioned is the land of al-Sham (Greater Syria) and the land of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). His saying: ﴿We sent against you servants of Ours⦆ – this sending is like His saying: ﴿Have We not sent the devils upon the disbelievers?﴾ It may mean empowerment (al-taslit, giving them dominion), and it may mean leaving a space between them and the people (al-takhliyah). The opinions differed about who they were.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: they were Jalut (Goliath) and his people. Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib said: Bukht Nassar (Nebuchadnezzar) the Persian. Another said: Sanhareeb (Sennacherib) the king. Some said: the Amalekites. The most apparent of the opinions is that it was Bukht Nassar. It is related from Mujahid that he said: four kings ruled the earth: two believers and two disbelievers. The believers were Sulayman and Dhu al-Qarnayn – peace be upon them both. The disbelievers were Namrud and Bukht Nassar.

The Shaykh, the Imam, the most Honoured said: This was related to us by Abu ʿAli al-Shafiʿi in Makkah, who said: Abu al-Hasan ibn Firas related to us, who said: Abu Jaʿfar Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Dibli related to us, who said: Saʿid ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Makhzumi related to us, who said: Sufyan ibn ʿUyaynah related to us, from Dawud ibn Shapur, from Mujahid.

His saying: ﴿people of great might⦆ means: people of strong power.

His saying: ﴿So they went through the habitations⦆ – al-jawas means seeking something thoroughly.

Al-Zajjaj said: they searched through the habitations to see whether anyone remained so that they might kill him. Khilal al-diyar means the midst of the habitations.

His saying: ﴿and it was a promise to be fulfilled⦆ means: a promise that must be carried out. The poet said:

(Fi al-jawas jasanna ilayka al-layl bi al-matiyy ...)

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 6:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then We gave you back your turn of victory over them﴾, i.e., the dynasty (al-dawla) over them. In the narrative, this destruction took place after the reign of Sulayman, and Bakht Nasr (Nebuchadnezzar) killed the fighting men, took the offspring captive, ruined Bayt al-Maqdis (the Holy House, Jerusalem), and threw carcasses into its mosque. Among the things that happened in this destruction was the death of the prophet Uzayr for a hundred years, and what Allah related of his affair in Surat al-Baqarah. Then Allah, exalted is He, restored the dynasty to the Children of Israel, so that they rebuilt what had been ruined.

In some narratives: Allah, exalted is He, sent an angel to them until he restored the buildings, rescued the captives, and the city returned better than it had been. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Then We gave you back your turn of victory over them﴾. As for the punishment of Bakht Nasr and his transformation, there is a long story, but this is not its place.

His saying: ﴿And We supplied you with wealth and children﴾ is clear in meaning. And His saying: ﴿And We made you more numerous in manpower﴾, i.e., more in number.

The poet said:

(And how noble is Qahtan as a people... and Himyar, how noble a people in manpower)

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 7:

The Exalted's saying: ﴿If you do good, you do good for your own selves﴾ means: you bring benefit to them.

And His saying: ﴿And if you do evil, it is against them﴾ means: upon them.

And His saying: ﴿So when the promise of the Hereafter comes﴾ means: the promise of the second time. And His saying: ﴿to disfigure your faces and to enter the mosque as they entered it the first time﴾ is recited thus; and it was recited: "to disfigure your faces" (ليسوء, with the short vowel), and from ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him): "to disfigure your faces" with the nun (لنسوء), which is the choice of al-Kisāʾī; and in the irregular readings: "to disfigure your faces" with a fatḥah on the lām (لنسوء). As for His saying ﴿to disfigure your faces﴾ with the yāʾ, it means: those people will disfigure your faces. And His saying ﴿to disfigure your faces﴾ means: so that the promise disfigures your faces.

And His saying "to disfigure" with the nun is clear in meaning, and the disfiguring of the face is by bringing grief and sorrow.

And His saying: ﴿and to destroy what they had gained with complete destruction﴾ means: to ruin and devastate what they had overpowered, i.e., what they had prevailed over, with destruction.

The poet said:

(And people are only two kinds: a doer who destroys what he builds, and another who raises.)

In the narrative: their second corruption was by the killing of Yaḥyā ibn Zakariyyā (peace be upon them both). The cause of his killing was that a prostitute of the Children of Israel asked the king to kill him, and so he killed him. When he was killed and his blood fell upon the ground, it began to boil and would not settle with anything, and Allah gave their enemy power over them.

It is said: the enemy in the second time was Bukhtnaṣr (Nebuchadnezzar), and in the first it was Jālūt (Goliath). It is also said: the enemy in the second time was a king of the Romans, who came and destroyed Bayt al-Maqdis, killed the fighters, and took the offspring captive.

It is related that he found it difficult to conquer the city. An old woman said: "O king, do you wish to conquer this city?" He said: "Yes." She said: "Say: O Allah, I ask You to open this city for me by the blood of Yaḥyā ibn Zakariyyā." He said these words, and the walls of the city collapsed; so he entered with the sword, killing, and reached the place where Yaḥyā's blood was boiling. He said: "I will certainly kill people upon it until the blood settles." So he killed forty thousand upon it, and it did not settle; he killed fifty thousand, and it did not settle; he killed sixty thousand, and it did not settle. He said: "By Allah, I will not cease killing upon it until it settles," and he completed seventy thousand, and it settled. It is also said: eighty thousand.

"And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It may be that your Lord will have mercy upon you; but if you return [to sin], We will return [to punishment].﴾ Mujahid said: "Perhaps" (ʿasā) from Allah is obligatory.

And His saying: ﴿that He will have mercy upon you﴾ means: that He will restore the dominion to you after its loss. In the account: Allah, Exalted is He, restored the dominion to them, and rebuilt Bayt al-Maqdis after it had been ruined, and your kingship returned to what it had been.

And His saying: ﴿but if you return, We will return﴾ its meaning is: if you return to disobedience, We will return to retribution. It is related from Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi that he said: "They returned to disobedience, so Allah took vengeance upon them through the Arabs, and they are subdued and humiliated until the Day of Resurrection." It was also said: [the retribution came] through Muhammad (ﷺ). The two opinions are close in meaning.

And His saying: ﴿And We have made Hell a prison (ḥaṣīr) for the disbelievers﴾. Mujahid said: "a place of confinement (maḥbas)." It was also said: ḥaṣīr means ḥāṣir (one who confines), an intensive form (faʿīl) in the sense of an active participle (fāʿil), as Ibn Qutayba stated.

Ḥaṣr means confinement (ḥabs), and prison is called ḥaṣīr in the language (lexicon)."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 9:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾. Concerning it there are two views. The first: it guides to the word that is most upright, where "aqwam" means "a'dal" (more just, more straight), and "the word" is the testimony that there is no god but Allah.

The second view, stated by al-Zajjaj: ﴿it guides to that which is most upright﴾, meaning: to the state that is most upright. The state that is most upright is the affirmation of Allah's oneness (tawhid), following His messengers, and obedience to His commands.

As for His saying: ﴿and gives good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds﴾, it means: the Qur'an gives good tidings to those who do righteous deeds.

And His saying: ﴿that for them is a great reward﴾, meaning: a magnificent one.

And [the words of Allah]: ﴿And that those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ means: "And give good tidings to those who do not believe in the Hereafter that We have ﴿prepared for them a painful punishment﴾." That is: We have prepared (a'dadna). Here "good tidings" (bushara) carries the meaning of "information" (khabar), because the Arabs do not place "good tidings" except in a context of joy.

The real meaning is: place this information for them in the position of good tidings.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 11:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And man prays for evil as he prays for good, and man has always been hasty.﴾ The prayer of a man for evil is that he invokes [harm] upon himself, his family and his children in a state of anger, so he says: "O Allah, destroy them! O Allah, curse them!" Perhaps he says this very same utterance to himself.

As for His saying, ﴿as he prays for good﴾, it means: like his prayer for good. It is said that this verse was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, for he said: "O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment."

So Allah answered him, and his neck was struck (in cold blood) on the day of Badr.

It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "O Allah, I am only a human being; I get angry as human beings get angry. Whichever Muslim I curse or revile, make that for him a means of prayer and mercy."

In some reports: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was brought a captive and he handed him over to Sawda bint Zam'a to keep him safe. The captive had come bound, and he kept moaning all night. Sawda got up and loosened his bonds, so the captive fled. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came in, he said to her: 'Where is the captive?' She told him what had happened, and he said: 'May Allah cut off your hand!' and he sent someone after the captive to bring him back. Sawda stretched out her hand, so that whoever came to cut it off would do so by the Prophet's supplication. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) entered upon her and saw her in that state, and asked her: 'Who is this?' She said: 'Because of your supplication, O Messenger of Allah.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'O Allah, I am only a human being; I get angry as human beings get angry...' " and the report continues.

His saying, ﴿and man has always been hasty﴾, means: he is hasty in calling for evil, and Allah does not hasten the answer.

There is another opinion regarding this verse, namely that it refers to Adam (peace be upon him). In the account: Allah placed the spirit in his head, and he began looking at himself, how he was being created! When the spirit reached his midsection, he wanted to stand up but could not, so Allah, Exalted is He, said: "And man was created hasty."

This is related from Qatadah and others. It is also reported from Salman al-Farisi that Allah created Adam in the last hour [of the day] ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs, and We effaced the sign of the night and made the sign of the day to give sight, that you may seek bounty from your Lord and that you may know the number of years and the reckoning﴾ on Friday. The spirit began to flow through his body, and Adam came to life and looked at the sun, which was setting, and said: "O Lord, [let it be] before the night" — that is, complete my creation before the night. Allah, Exalted is He, said: "And man was created hasty."

There is another view regarding the original meaning of the verse: that His saying ﴿And man prays for evil﴾ means he prays for committing sin just as he prays for performing obedience. The poet said:

(Perhaps the reliever of distress concerning Yusuf will subjugate to me the lady of the litter.)

But the correct view is what we presented earlier.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 12:

His saying: ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs﴾ means: two signs indicating that they have one God.

It is also said: two signs of the night and the day, and what is meant by the night and the day is the sun and the moon.

As for His saying: ﴿So We effaced the sign of the night﴾, it was narrated from ʿAli and Ibn ʿAbbas that they both said: the effacement is the blackness that is in the moon.

In some reports, Ibn al-Kawwa stood up before ʿAli and asked him about this, and he said: "A blind man (he meant blindness of the heart) asks about one who is blind!" Then he said: "It is the blackness that is in the moon." It is also said that the meaning of His saying: ﴿So We effaced the sign of the night﴾ is: We made the night such that one cannot see in it, just as one cannot see writing when it has been erased.

Qatadah and a group of the exegetes, and this is also related from Ibn ʿAbbas, said: God Most High created the sun and the moon both shining and luminous, each of them like the other in brightness, so that people could not tell the night from the day nor the day from the night. So He commanded Jibril, and he wiped the face of the moon with his wing.

Muqatil said: there was removed from it sixty-nine parts, and one part remained.

His saying: ﴿And We made the sign of the day to be seeing﴾ means: bright and radiant. It is also said: possessing sight, that is, one sees by it.

His saying: ﴿that you may seek bounty from your Lord﴾ means: during the day.

His saying: ﴿and that you may know the number of years and the reckoning﴾ means: the number of years and the reckoning of months and days.

His saying: ﴿And every thing We have detailed with full detail﴾ means: We have explained it with clear explanation.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 13:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And every person We have fastened his bird (ṭā'ir) to his neck﴾. ʿAṭāʾ related from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: its meaning is what has been decreed for him of good and evil.

And from Mujāhid: his deeds, of good and evil. And from al-Ḍaḥḥāk: his term of life, his provision, his happiness and his misery. And from Abū ʿUbayda he said: his share (ḥaẓẓ). It has also been said: his book.

And from Mujāhid in another narration: a paper hanging from his neck, in which is written whether he is wretched or happy. The statements are close in meaning. It is only called a "bird" (ṭā'ir), meaning that which has flown for him of good or evil, and this is by way of illustration and analogy. From this comes the notion of the sāniḥ and the bāriḥ: the sāniḥ is the bird that flies from the right, by which a person takes omen of blessing, and the bāriḥ is the bird that flies from the left, by which a person takes omen of ill fortune. The poet said:

(The locks of polytheism fly away, in pairs and singly, and leadership belongs to the boy.)

His saying: ﴿And We will bring forth for him on the Day of Resurrection﴾. It was read: "wa-yukhraju lahu" with the yā', meaning the bird comes forth for him. It was also read: "wa-yukhraju lahu yawm al-qiyāma kitāb" in the passive voice, not naming the agent. It was also read "wa-yakhruju" with a fatḥa on the yā', meaning: his deed comes forth ﴿as a book﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, as if the deed transforms into a book on the Resurrection.

His saying: ﴿He will meet it﴾. Al-Ḥasan read "yulqāhu" with a ḍamma on the yā', from the causative (tilqiya), and this is an anomalous reading (shādh).

His saying: ﴿Spread open﴾. It is reported in the traditions that God, may He be exalted, commands the two angels to fold up the scroll when the servant's lifespan is complete, so that it is not unfolded until the Day of Resurrection, and this is in the sense of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when the scrolls are unfolded﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 14:

His saying: ﴿Read your book.﴾ There is an ellipsis (idmar) in it, namely that it will be said to him: "Read your book." Qatadah said: Every person will read it, whether he was a reader in the world or was not a reader.

And His saying: ﴿Sufficient is your own soul against you this Day as a reckoner (hasib).﴾ That is: as a witness. Al-Hasan said: "He has been just with you, the One who made you the reckoner of your own soul."

Some of them said: It will be said to him, "This is a book whose pen was your tongue, whose ink was your saliva, and whose paper was your limbs; and the one who dictated it was the one who wrote it down on your two scribes. So read what you dictated. And God knows best."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 15:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whoever is guided, is only guided for [the benefit of] his own soul﴾. That is, the benefit of his being guided accrues to him.

And His saying: ﴿And whoever goes astray, only goes astray to its detriment﴾. That is, the harm of his straying falls upon him.

And His saying: ﴿No bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾. It is said: this verse was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, for he said to those who had embraced Islam: "Return to your former religion, and I will bear your burdens." So God, Exalted is He, revealed this verse. Its meaning is that no one is held accountable for another's sin. It was also said: no one has the right to commit a sin and then say, "So-and-so has sinned, so I will follow him," for I do not hold anyone accountable for the sin of another.

And His saying: ﴿And We would never punish until We have sent a messenger﴾. This is evidence that what is obligatory is made obligatory by revelation (al-sam', i.e. scriptural transmission) and not by reason (al-'aql), for God, Exalted is He, has explicitly stated that He does not punish anyone until He sends a Messenger.

In some of the musnads, from Abu Hurayrah, he said: On the Day of Resurrection, God, Exalted is He, will raise up the people of the fatrah (the interval between prophets), the mentally deficient (al-ma'tuh), the deaf, the mute, the dumb-mute, and the elderly who did not reach Islam. A fire will be kindled for them, and He will say: "Enter it." They will say: "How can we enter it, when You did not send a messenger to us?" Had they entered it, it would have been cool and safe for them. Then God will send a messenger to them, and whoever God knows would obey him will obey him, and whoever God knows would disobey him will disobey him. Thus He will separate them on that basis.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 16:

The Almighty's saying: ﴿When We intend to destroy a town﴾, meaning: the people of a town. It is also recited ﴿amarna mutrafeeha﴾, and this is the well-known reading. It is also recited "āmarnā" with a long vowel, "mutrafīhā," and this is reported from ʿAlī. It was also recited "amarnā" with short vowel and shaddah, and it was recited "amarnā" with a kasrah on the mīm, "mutrafīhā," and this is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās.

As for His saying ﴿amarnā﴾, there are two opinions. The first: its meaning is "We commanded them to obedience, so they committed sin and disobeyed."

This is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbās and a group of the Successors (tābiʿūn), among them Ibn Jurayj and others.

The second opinion: "amarnā" means "we increased them," as it is said: "amara al-qawm" when the people became numerous. The poet said:

(If they are envied, they descend; and if they multiply ... one day they will go to ruin and misery.)

Al-Kisāʾī denied that "amarnā" could mean "akthharnā" (we increased them), and said: "It is āmarnā in the sense of akthharnā, and this is the prevailing dialect."

As for Abū ʿUbayda, he said: The Arabs say "amarnā" in the sense of "akthharnā." We only needed this interpretation because God, exalted is He, does not command sins.

This is by the consensus of the community (ummah). There is a well-known question regarding the verse: it is said, how does He command its affluent people to wickedness, when God, exalted is He, says: ﴿Indeed, God commands justice and good conduct﴾, and says: {Indeed, God does not command indecency}? The answer is what has already been given.

There is a third opinion in the verse, that the meaning of His saying ﴿amarnā mutrafīhā﴾ is "We sent," and in the reading of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: "When We intend to destroy a town, We send its affluent people." As for His saying "amarnā" with shaddah, it means "We empowered."

It was also said: "amarnā" means "We made them commanders," so it is permissible that it means "We sent" in this sense.

As for "amarnā" with a kasrah on the mīm, they have mentioned that it is weak in the language.

His saying ﴿mutrafīhā﴾ means "those given luxury," and the mutraf is the wealthy, pampered king; this was reported by Thaʿlab.

His saying ﴿fa-fasaqū fīhā﴾ means "they disobeyed therein." ﴿Fa-ḥaqqa ʿalayhā al-qawl﴾ means "the word became binding upon it," i.e., the punishment became due upon it.

His saying ﴿fa-dammarnāhā tadmīrā﴾ means "We destroyed it with complete destruction."

Almighty God's words: ﴿And how many generations have We destroyed after Noah?﴾ The scholars differed regarding the word qarn (generation). Some of them said: a qarn is one hundred and twenty years; some said: one hundred years; some said: eighty years; and some said: forty years. And what is meant by "the generations" is the people of the generations.

As for His words: ﴿And your Lord is sufficient as one who is All-Aware of the sins of His servants, All-Seeing,﴾ its meaning is apparent.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 18:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whoever desires the hastened [good]﴾, meaning: the worldly life (al-dunya). This is a description of the disbelievers, because they are the ones who desire the worldly life and do not desire the Hereafter. The verse concerns a people who desired only the hastened [good].

And His saying: ﴿We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We intend﴾, meaning: for whom We intend to destroy.

And His saying: ﴿Then We have made Hell for him; he will burn therein﴾, meaning: he will enter it. It was also said: he will suffer its heat.

And His saying: ﴿Blamed and banished﴾. The madhmum (blamed) is from blame (dhamm), and the madhhur (banished) is the one expelled and removed far from the mercy of Allah. It is said: "daharahu" from such-and-such, meaning he removed him far away.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 19:

The Exalted's saying: ﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter﴾, i.e., seeks the Hereafter, ﴿and strives for it with the striving due to it while he is a believer﴾, i.e., he performs its deeds, and he is a believer.

And His saying: ﴿those are the ones whose striving is appreciated﴾, i.e., accepted.

It is said: indeed, gratitude (shukr) from Allah is the acceptance of good deeds and the overlooking of misdeeds. And it has been said that the meaning of the verse is: He places their deeds in the position for which they are thanked.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 20:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿To each — these and those — We extend﴾, means: the believers and the disbelievers.

And His saying: ﴿from the bounty of your Lord﴾, means: from the provision of your Lord.

And His saying: ﴿And the bounty of your Lord is never withheld﴾, means: never prevented.

The people of tafsir (tafsir, exegesis of the Qur'an) have agreed that the meaning of "the bounty of your Lord" in this surah is the worldly life, for the Hereafter belongs to the God-fearing, and the disbelievers have no share in it.

And in some of the musnads (musnad, hadith collections arranged by narrator) it is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed God has apportioned among you your characters just as He has apportioned among you your provisions, and indeed God Most High gives the world to whomever He loves and to whomever He does not love, but He gives religion only to whomever He loves."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 21:

His the Exalted's saying: ﴿Look how We have favoured some of them over others﴾. He means: in this world. The meaning of tafdil (favouring) here is restriction and expansion, reduction and increase, and withholding and extending. It has been narrated in some reports that Allah the Exalted presented the offspring of Adam to Adam, and he saw among them great disparity, so he said: "My Lord, why did You not make Your creation equal?" He said: "O Adam, I wished to be thanked."

As for His saying: ﴿And the Hereafter is greater in degrees﴾, we have already explained that a daraja (degree) is the distance between the heaven and the earth.

In some of the musnad collections, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "Paradise has one hundred degrees; between each two degrees is five hundred years."

As for His saying: ﴿And greater in preference﴾, meaning: greater in favouring.

In the reports, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the believers enter Paradise by their faith, and they divide the degrees by their deeds."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 22:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do not set up with God another god﴾, concerning which there are two opinions. The first: the address is to the Messenger, and what is meant is the community (ummah), and we have already explained a similar case before.

The other opinion: "Do not set up, O human being, with God another god," and this address is to everyone.

It was also said: what is meant is the Prophet (ﷺ), as is the apparent meaning. Even though he is protected from error (ma'sum), the address is not lifted from him by way of guarding against and keeping far from disbelief.

And His saying: ﴿So you will sit reproached, forsaken﴾, meaning: reproached without praise, and forsaken without help.

﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and that you be good to parents. Whether one or both of them reach old age with you...﴾

It was also said: "forsaken" means abandoned by protection, and when God abandons a servant, He has destroyed him.

And the meaning of His saying: ﴿So you will sit﴾ is: so you will be deprived (ma'fuk), and remain forsaken.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 23:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud recited: "And your Lord has enjoined (wassa) that you worship none but Him." Al-Dahhak said: Originally it was "wassa," but the waw became joined to the sad in writing, so it was read "qada" (decreed). The well-known reading is His saying "qada," and the readers are in agreement upon it. Its meaning is: "and your Lord commanded." The true meaning of qada (decree) is the firm establishing of a thing and its execution in such a way that it is finished, and from this is the saying of people: the judge (qadi) decided between the two litigants. And from it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then carry out your plan against me and give me no respite﴾, meaning: empty what is in your souls and carry it out. Accordingly, the meaning of His saying ﴿And your Lord has decreed﴾ is: your Lord has ruled over them with a ruling of worship.

The sense of "completion" here is the completion of worship. In some exegeses it is related that a man came to al-Hasan al-Basri and said: "I divorced my wife three times." He said: "You have disobeyed your Lord, and your wife has become separated from you." The man said: "Was that the decree of God?" Al-Hasan said: "You lie; God did not decree that." That is: God did not command that. Al-Hasan was eloquent, but people did not understand his words, so they reported that he denies predestination.

In some narrations it is said that he was told: "The Banu Umayyah kill people and say: 'This is the decree of God.'" Al-Hasan said: "The enemies of God lie." Its meaning is what we have explained.

It is also said that he denied their making that a cause for their killing; this was mentioned by Ibn Qutaybah in al-Ma'arif.

His saying: ﴿that you worship none but Him﴾ means: that you affirm His unity and do not associate anything with Him. His saying: ﴿and to parents, good treatment﴾ means: He commanded that you treat your parents well.

It has been established from the Prophet, through the narration of Ibn Mas'ud, that he asked the Messenger of God: "Which sin is greatest?" He said: "Associating partners with God." He said: "Then which?" He said: "Disobedience to parents."

His saying: ﴿If one of them or both reach old age with you﴾. It was also read: "If they reach old age with you (yablughanna 'indaka al-kibar)." So His saying ﴿reach (yablughan)﴾ refers to both of them; in this case His saying ﴿one of them or both﴾ is a new (independent) clause. His saying ﴿reach (yablughan)﴾ refers to one of them, so His saying ﴿or both﴾ is in apposition to it.

His saying: ﴿So do not say to them "uff"﴾. It was read: "uff" with a kasra on the fa', "uff" with a fatha on the fa', and "uff" with a kasra and tanwin. They said: there are six dialectal forms of it: uffan, uffun, uffin (all three with tanwin), and uff, uffu, uffi without tanwin.

Al-Asma'i said: the uff is the wax of the ear, and the tuff is the dirt of the nails. It is also said: the uff is the dirt of the nails, and the tuff is a small thing. Its real meaning is that it is a word said at the time of irritation with a thing and finding it burdensome. It is also said: the uff is the least degree of being vexed by something. So the meaning of the verse is: do not be vexed by them, and do not find it burdensome to bear their harm. Mujahid mentioned that it refers to the time of excrement and urine and their owner: that you do not find it burdensome to tend to them in that, just as they did not find it burdensome to tend to you.

His saying: ﴿and do not reproach them (wa la tanharhuma)﴾. Al-intihar is from the nahr, which is rebuking with harshness and shouting.

His saying: ﴿and speak to them a generous word (qaulan kariman)﴾ means: a gentle word.

From Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Baqir, he said: The worst of fathers is one whom righteousness drives to excess, and the worst of sons is one whom negligence drives to disobedience.

From 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, he said: If God had known of anything more forceful in rebuke than His saying "uff," He would have forbidden it. Then 'Ali said: Let the dutiful do whatever he wishes, he will never enter the Fire; and let the disobedient do whatever he wishes, he will never enter Paradise.

In the reports from the Prophet, he said: "Righteousness increases the lifespan." Muslim mentioned in his Sahih, through the narration of Suhayl from his father from Abu Hurayrah, that the Prophet said: "May he be humiliated! May he be humiliated! May he be humiliated!" It was asked: "Who, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Whoever reaches his parents in old age, or one of them, and does not enter Paradise."

Amir ibn Rabi'ah narrated that a man came to the Prophet and said: "My parents have both died; is there anything I can still do to show them kindness?" He said: "Yes: carrying out their covenant, honouring their friends, asking forgiveness for them, and giving charity on their behalf."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 24:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy﴾ mean: soften your side toward them.

And it is reported from ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she said: "Obey them in what they command you." Al-khafḍ (lowering) is humility (tawāḍuʿ), and janāḥ al-dhull (the wing of humility) is abandoning self-elevation (istiʿlāʾ). It is taken from a bird's elevating itself [with its wings].

His words ﴿out of mercy﴾ mean: out of compassion and tenderness.

ʿĀṣim al-Jaḥdarī and Yaḥyā ibn Dithār recited: "wa-ikhfiḍ lahumā janāḥ al-dhill" with a kasra on the dhāl. Al-dhull (with a ḍamma on the dhāl) comes from tadhallul (abasement), meaning: be to them like one who is humbled and subdued. Al-dhill (with a kasra on the dhāl) comes from submission (inqiyād) and obedience (ṭāʿa).

It is reported from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib that he said: "Be before them like a sinful slave before a harsh, coarse master."

His words ﴿And say: My Lord, have mercy on them as they raised me when I was small﴾ mean: as they showed mercy to me by raising me when I was young.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 25:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Your Lord knows best what is in your souls﴾, i.e., what is in your hearts. And His saying: ﴿If you are righteous﴾, i.e., obedient.

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, He is ever Forgiving to the often-returning (awwabin)﴾. The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Your Lord knows best what is in your souls﴾ of disobedience to parents (uquq) and of righteousness. So if a righteous person commits a lapse of disobedience, then indeed God is ever Forgiving to the awwabin, meaning: ﴿to the repentant (tawwabin)﴾ Forgiving.

Regarding the awwab (awwab, one who constantly turns back to God in repentance) there are many sayings. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: it is the one who returns from evil to good. And from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib: it is the one who, whenever he sins, repents, however often that happens. And from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr: it is the one who does not rise from a gathering until he seeks forgiveness of God for his sins. It was also said: the awwab is the one who glorifies God (musabbih), God, exalted is He, said: ﴿O mountains, echo His praise with him (awwibi ma'ahu)﴾. And from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, he said: the awwab is the one who prays between Maghrib and 'Isha', and the prayer at that time is called the prayer of the awwabin. And from 'Awn al-'Uqayli, he said: the awwab is the one who prays the Duha (forenoon) prayer. And from al-Suddi, he said: it is the one who sins secretly and repents secretly.

The origin of awwab is the one who returns (al-raji'). The poet said:

(Two days: a day of standing in assemblies and ransoming, and a day of marching against the enemies, returning (ta'wib).)

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 26:

The word of the Exalted: ﴿And give to the near of kin his right﴾. Most of the scholars hold that "dhu al-qurba" (the near of kin) here means a person's relatives, and the meaning of the verse is a command to maintain ties of kinship (silat al-arham) with those related by blood.

It is narrated from Ali ibn al-Husayn, who said: "Dhu al-qurba here means the relatives of the Messenger" (ﷺ).

His word: ﴿and the needy﴾, that is, the beggar who goes around asking.

His word: ﴿and the wayfarer﴾. It was said: the one cut off from his means of travel; and it was said: the guest.

His word: ﴿and do not squander wastefully﴾, that is, do not spend extravagantly.

Tabdhir (wasteful squandering) is spending in other than obedience to Allah the Exalted. It is narrated from Uthman ibn al-Aswad, who said: "I was circumambulating the House with Mujahid when he said: If a man spent ten thousand dirhams in obedience to Allah, he would not be a spendthrift; and if he spent a single dirham in disobedience to Allah, he would be among the spendthrifts."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 27:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the squanderers are brothers of the devils﴾, i.e., they are like the devils (ashbah al-shayatin). It was also said: He called them "brothers of the devils" because they followed what the devils embellished for them, and [it was also said] to one who follows a person in a matter, he is his brother (akhuhu) in it.

And His saying: ﴿And the devil was ever ungrateful to his Lord﴾, i.e., disbelieving in his Lord.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 28:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And if you turn away from them﴾. Al-i'rad (turning away) is turning the face away from something (...) or toward one who is better than it, or to humiliate the one from whom the face is turned away.

And His words: ﴿seeking mercy from your Lord﴾, meaning: seeking provision from your Lord.

And His words: ﴿for which you hope﴾. Al-raja' (hope) is the soul attaching itself to the one from whom good is sought. It is reported from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: Do not hope for anything except from your Lord, and do not fear anything except from your Lord.

And His words: ﴿then speak to them a gentle word﴾. Al-yusr (ease) is the opposite of hardship, and al-maysur here is the promise, according to the view of most of the exegetes. It is that one says: something will come to us and we will give it to you. It is reported from Sufyan al-Thawri that he said: The promise of a Prophet is a debt. It was also said: the gentle word is that you say: may Allah provide for us and for you, or he says: may Allah bless you.

Know that the verse is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ). These people used to ask him, and he disliked refusing them while he had nothing to give, so he would remain silent. Then Allah the Exalted revealed this verse: ﴿then speak to them a gentle word﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 29:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾ – the verse (to its end). Ibn Mas'ud related that a woman sent a boy to the Messenger of Allah asking him for something. The Prophet said: "I have nothing." The boy returned and told her. So she sent the boy back and said: "Ask him for his shirt which he is wearing." He asked him, and he gave it to him, and he remained in the house without a shirt. So Allah, may He be exalted, revealed this verse.

His saying: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾, meaning: do not be stingy. The speech is in the form of a metaphor, so the miserly, withholding person is likened to one whose hand is chained to his neck.

His saying: ﴿And do not spread it out completely open﴾, meaning: do not be extravagant in giving.

His saying: ﴿Lest you sit blamed and destitute﴾. The one blamed (malum) is the one who has done that for which he blames himself and for which others blame him. The destitute (mahsur) is the one who is cut off, whose wealth has gone and who remains in regret. It is said: "a beast is hasir (exhausted) when it has become weary from travel and has thrown its rider." So the meaning of the verse is: do not burden yourself completely in giving, so that you become like one who has reached the extreme of fatigue and exhaustion.

Qatadah said: "Mahsuran" means: regretful. And they cited, concerning the exhausted beast (al-hasir):

(Its rooster is exhausted... as for its bones, they are white... as for its skin, it is hard.)

Almost the entire commentary here is a single line: the verse, followed by a brief remark.

God's words, "Indeed your Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it. Indeed He is ever, of His servants, All-Knowing, All-Seeing": the meaning is apparent, and we have already explained the meaning of extending (al-bast) and measuring out (al-qadr) earlier.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty﴾, meaning: for fear of poverty. They used to bury their daughters alive for fear of poverty.

And His words: ﴿We provide for them and for you﴾, meaning: it is We who grant provision, not you.

And His words: ﴿Indeed, their killing is a great sin﴾. The commonly known reading is "khiṭan" (khiṭ'an) with a kasra on the kha and without a madd. Ibn Kathir read "khiṭā'an" with a kasra and a madd. Ibn 'Amir read "khaṭa'an" with a fatha on the kha and the ta and without a madd. It was also read "khaṭā'an" with a fatha and a madd.

As for "khiṭa'" with a kasra and no madd, it means: a great sin (ithman kabiran). As for "khiṭā'" with a kasra and a madd, al-Azhari said: the people of the language do not know this! Perhaps it is a dialect (lughah).

As for "khaṭā'" with a fatha and no madd, it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) like "akhṭa'a" (to err). The difference between khiṭa' and khaṭa', both without madd, is that khiṭa' (with kasra) is what is committed deliberately, and its doer is sinful, while khaṭa' (with fatha) is what is not committed deliberately. They recited in verse:

(Servants who err, and You are a Lord ... Generous, not befitting You is reproach.)

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 32:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not approach adultery﴾. Its meaning is apparent.

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is an abomination﴾. Al-fahisha (abomination): an act that is ugly in the most ugly of its aspects.

And His saying: ﴿And evil is it as a way﴾. That is: it is evil as a path, and its meaning is that this act is a wretched course (sulk, "way/path") to take.

In some reports, with a narration from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Adultery has six characteristics: three in this world and three in the Hereafter. As for the three in this world: it removes the light of the face, it brings about poverty, and it shortens the lifespan. As for the three in the Hereafter: the anger of the Lord, a poor reckoning, and entry into the Fire."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 33:

The Most High's words: ﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right﴾. It is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The blood of a Muslim man is not lawful except in one of three cases: disbelief after belief, an adulterer who is married (al-thayyib al-zani), and one who kills a soul without right."

So His words ﴿except by right﴾: killing by right is that it occurs in one of these three things.

His words: ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have given his heir authority﴾, meaning: the authority of retaliation (al-qawad). This is what Qatadah and others said. It is related from al-Dahhak that the authority here is the choice given to the heir of the slain between killing, pardoning, or taking the blood-money (al-diyah).

The original meaning of sultan is proof (al-hujjah). When this was established for the heir of the slain by a clear proof, He called it sultan. It was also said: the meaning of the verse is that the heir may kill; and if there is no heir, the ruler (al-sultan) kills.

His words: ﴿but let him not commit excess in killing﴾. Most of the exegetes hold that excess in killing is that one kills someone other than the killer. It was also said: excess in killing is that one mutilates the slain. It is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: Excess in killing is that one seeks to kill a group for one person. The Jahiliyyah would not be content with killing the killer alone when the slain was of noble status, and they would seek to kill the killer together with a group of his relatives and people.

It was recited: "fa-la tasrif" with the ta' (addressing the heir of the slain), and "fa-la yasrif" with the ya' (in the third person). There is another opinion regarding the verse, namely that the meaning of His words ﴿let him not commit excess in killing﴾ with the ya' is: the first killer, the transgressor.

His words: ﴿Indeed, he is ever supported﴾ according to this view mean that if the first killer transgresses, the heir of the slain is supported by Me. The people of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) have said that the meaning of His words ﴿indeed, he is ever supported﴾ is: the slain is supported in this world and the Hereafter. As for support in this world, it is in the obligation of retaliation for him. As for support in the Hereafter, it is by the expiation of his sins and by the obligation of vengeance for his killer. It was also said: ﴿indeed, he was supported﴾ means the heir of the slain.

Abu ibn Ka'b recited: "fa-la tasrifu fi'l-qatl inna waliyya'l-qatili kana mansuran."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 34:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the way that is best﴾ means: except with the best conduct (al-'iffah allati hiya ahsan). The scholars differed about its meaning, giving several opinions. The first: approaching it in the best way is preserving the principal and making its offshoots grow. The second: approaching it in the best way is trading with his wealth, and this is close to the first. The third opinion: approaching it in the best way is not mixing the orphan's property with one's own property.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that when this verse was revealed, the guardians separated their food from the orphans' food and their drink from the orphans' drink, and they would withhold the orphan's food until it was eaten or spoiled. So Allah, may He be exalted, revealed: ﴿And if you mix with them, they are your brothers﴾.

It is narrated from Mujahid that he said: approaching it in the best way is that one may borrow from the orphan's property when he is in need of it, and when he becomes wealthy, he returns it.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: one should not approach his property at all, nor drink water from his property.

Some scholars, among them Abu Yusuf, held that His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever is wealthy, let him abstain; and whoever is poor, let him eat in a reasonable manner﴾ has been abrogated (mansukh) by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who believe, do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood, except that it be trade by mutual consent among you﴾. We have already mentioned on this matter earlier what is more than this.

As for His saying: ﴿until he reaches his maturity (ashuddahu)﴾, most scholars hold that ashudd is the age of maturity of intellect (al-hilm). Some said it is eighteen years, and some said thirty-three years; this is the time of the peak of strength and the completion of reason through experience and seasoned judgment.

As for His saying: ﴿And fulfill the covenant﴾, Qatadah said: the covenant is everything that Allah, may He be exalted, has commanded and forbidden.

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, the covenant will be questioned﴾, there are several opinions regarding it. The first: that it was wronged (madhlum), and this is the view of al-Suddi. The second: that it will be asked about (mas'ul 'anhu), and this is the best of the opinions. The third: that the covenant is questioned about its party, so it is said to him: "Why did you break it?", like the buried infant girl who will be asked, "For what sin was she killed?"

And regarding the meaning of the covenant there is another opinion: that it is everything a person binds himself to.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 35:

The Almighty's saying: ﴿Give full measure when you measure﴾ — its meaning is apparent.

And His saying: ﴿and weigh with the true balance﴾ — concerning it there are two opinions: the first is that it is the qabban (the steelyard, a lever-type balance), and the other is that it is any balance that exists. This was related by al-Zajjaj.

They differed over whether al-Qistas (the balance) is Roman or Arabic. Mujahid said: it is Roman, arabicized (mu'arrab). Others said: ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart — about all those one will be questioned﴾ — it is Arabic, derived from al-qist, and al-qist is justice. Accordingly, the meaning of the verse is: weigh with true justice.

And His saying: ﴿That is better﴾ — meaning: that is better for you in this world through good repute. ﴿And better in outcome﴾ — meaning: better in final result in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 36:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge﴾. They said: its meaning is "And do not say that of which you have no knowledge." It was also recited as "And do not pursue (taqfu) that of which you have no knowledge," with the qaf raised (wa la taqfu, with damma); its meaning is what we have mentioned. Among them are those who said: the meaning of His saying ﴿And do not pursue﴾ is: do not throw out by conjecture that of which you have no knowledge. The origin of qiyafah (tracking, physiognomic judgment) is following a trace; it is said: "qafawtu fulanan" (I followed so-and-so) when I [followed] his track. The real meaning is: do not let your tongue follow that of which you have no knowledge, so that it speaks by guesswork and supposition.

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "We are the sons of an-Nadr ibn Kinanah; we do not trace our mother (lā naqfu ummanā), nor do we disown our father."

In some reports the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever pursues (taqawwafa) that of which he has no knowledge will be detained in radghat al-khabal (the pus of the people of Hell) until he comes out of what he said."

His saying: ﴿Indeed, the hearing and the sight and the heart﴾. It is related from Qatadah that he said: Do not say "I heard" when you did not hear, nor "I saw" when you did not see, nor "I knew" when you did not know. There is disagreement concerning the questioning of the hearing, the sight and the heart. In one of the two opinions: a person will be questioned about his hearing, his sight and his heart.

The second opinion: the hearing, the sight and the heart will be questioned about what the person did. If it is said: He has said ﴿all those were questioned about﴾, and "those" is not used except for rational beings? The answer: We say it is permissible to use it for non-rational beings. Jarir said:

(Blaming the dwellings after the abode of al-Liwa ... and life after those days)

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 37:

The Exalted's saying: ﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly.﴾ Al-marah (exultation) is joy in falsehood. It is also said: it is insolence and arrogance (al-ashar wa al-batar). It is also said: it is boastfulness and greatness (al-ba'w wa al-'azamah). And it is said: it is self-conceit (al-khuyala').

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, you will never tear through the earth﴾, meaning: you will never pierce the earth. It is also said: you will never cross the earth by travelling.

And His saying: ﴿And you will never reach the mountains in height﴾, meaning: no one can make the mountains grow taller. There are two interpretations of this meaning. The first: when a person walks in self-conceit, sometimes he walks on his heels and sometimes he walks on the front of his feet. So it says: you will never pierce the earth if you walk on your heels, and you will never reach the mountains in height if you walk on the front of your feet.

The second interpretation: whoever wishes to tear through the earth or to rival the mountains will not achieve anything, and likewise whoever walks in self-conceit will not achieve anything by his self-conceit.

The Qur'anic phrase: ﴿All of that was evil, hateful in the sight of your Lord.﴾

And His saying: ﴿كل ذلك كان سيئة عند ربك مكروها﴾ is read as "sayyi'ah" (with the tanwin, the nunation). His saying "sayyi'atan" (with tanwin) means: everything that You have been forbidden from in these verses, it is evil and hateful in the sight of your Lord. As for the one who reads "sayyi'atuhu" with the raf' (nominative, without tanwin, as "sayyi'atuhu"), its meaning is partitive (ʿalā al-tab'īḍ, "of a part"), because some of what is not evil has already been mentioned, such as His saying: ﴿And give the near of kin his right﴾, and likewise His saying: ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy and say, "My Lord, have mercy upon them as they brought me up when I was small."﴾, and other than that. So its meaning is that what has preceded in these verses of evil is hateful in the sight of your Lord.

That is the (divine) wisdom which your Lord has revealed to you. Whatever God has commanded and forbidden is wisdom.

And His words: "Do not set up with God another god, lest you be cast into Hell, blameworthy and rejected." We have already explained this before, that the address is directed to him (the Prophet ﷺ), while what is meant is the community (ummah).

And His words: "Then you will be cast into Hell, blameworthy, rejected," i.e., expelled (maṭrūdan).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 40:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Has your Lord then chosen for you sons and taken for Himself daughters from the angels?﴾ Its meaning is: Has He then chosen for you the best, and assigned to Himself what is not the best? This is in the form of a rebuke (inkar), for they used to say: the angels are the daughters of God.

And His saying: ﴿with sons, and has taken for Himself females from the angels﴾ — this is its meaning.

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, you utter a tremendous saying﴾ — i.e., monstrous, great.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 41:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We have certainly diversified in this Qur'an﴾, there are two views concerning it. One of them: the repetition of commands, prohibitions, admonitions and narratives. The other: the clarification of the speech in all its aspects.

His saying: ﴿that they may remember﴾ means: that they may take heed.

His saying: ﴿but it increases them only in aversion﴾ means: the clarification increases them only in aversion. It was also said: [it means] the variation of speech in commands and prohibitions.

"His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: If there were with Him other gods﴾, that is: with God, ﴿gods﴾.

And His saying: ﴿as they say, then they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne﴾. Concerning it there are two opinions. The first: then they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne by drawing near to Him. The second, and it is the more correct: then they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne by contention and rivalry, and by seeking dominion. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than God, they would both have been ruined﴾."
His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Glory be to Him, and exalted is He far above what they say.﴾ Its meaning is apparent.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 44:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The seven heavens and the earth praise Him, and whoever is in them﴾ — we have explained this before.

And His saying: ﴿And there is not a thing but exalts His praise﴾. Ikrimah said: "And there is not a thing that is living but exalts His praise." And from Ikrimah also, he said: "The tree glorifies Him."

And from Mujahid, he said: "All things glorify God, whether living or inanimate, and their glorification is (Subhan Allah wa bihamdihi, 'Glory be to God and praise be to Him')."

And from Abu Salih, that he heard the creaking of a door and said: "That is its glorification."

And from Ali, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "Do not strike the beasts on their heads, for they glorify God." And from Ibn Abbas: "The glorification of these things is: 'O Forbearing, O Forgiving.'"

Mansur ibn al-Mu'tamir Abu Ghiyath narrated from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, who said: "'And there is not a thing, inanimate or living, but exalts His praise,' even the creaking of the door and the creaking of the ceiling."

Know that God has a knowledge concerning the inanimate that no one else knows and no one else comprehends, so it is fitting to leave its knowledge to Him. Some of the scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: the glorification of the heavens, the earth, the inanimate things, and all the animals other than the rational ones, is what they indicate, through the subtlety of their composition and the wonder of their forms, of their Creator, and so this becomes like glorification from them.

What is transmitted from the early generations (al-salaf) is what we have stated before, and God knows best.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But you do not understand their glorification﴾ — meaning: you do not know their glorification.

And from al-Hasan al-Basri, that the place of this verse in the Torah is a thousand verses, in which God, exalted is He, said: "Glorify Me with such-and-such, glorify Me with such-and-such, glorify Me with such-and-such." And according to the last opinion, His saying ﴿But you do not understand their glorification﴾ means: you do not derive proof from observing these things concerning the magnification of God. This is not a reliable view, and the correct one is what we have explained.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, He is ever Forbearing, Forgiving﴾ — we have explained the meaning of al-Halim (the Forbearing) and al-Ghafur (the Forgiving).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 45:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a hidden barrier﴾. It is related in the reports that when the surah ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﴾ was revealed, his wife Umm Jamil came to him carrying a stone, and she made for the Prophet while saying: "We have disobeyed the one who is reviled, we have denied his religion, and we have rebelled against his command." The Prophet was sitting with Abu Bakr in the Hijr, so Abu Bakr said to the Prophet: "This woman has come." The Prophet said: "Indeed, she will not see me," and he recited this verse. The woman came and said: "O Abu Bakr, where is your companion? It has reached me that he has satirized me and satirized Abu Lahab, and the Quraysh know that I am the daughter of their chief." Abu Bakr said nothing, and she returned saying: "You have indeed brought this stone so that I may crush his head." Narrated by Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her.

Some scholars said: the Prophet was praying and reciting the Qur'an, and the polytheists intended to harm him, so they would come but not see him.

As for His saying, ﴿a hidden barrier﴾, there are two views: the first is that it is a concealing barrier (ḥijāban sātiran); the second is that it is a barrier by which he is concealed (mastūran bihi). It has also been said that the barrier which Allah made is the coverings (akinnah) which He created upon their hearts.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 46:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings (akinna)﴾, meaning: coverings. One of the early scholars (al-salaf) related that he heard a man recite: ﴿And what prevented the people from believing when the guidance came to them﴾, and he said: "al-akinna" (the coverings).

And His saying: ﴿lest they understand it (an yafqahuhu)﴾, its meaning is: out of aversion that they understand it. It was also said: so that they do not understand it.

And His saying: ﴿and in their ears a deafness (waqran)﴾, meaning: a heaviness, and its meaning: so that they do not hear it. In this verse there is a clear refutation of the Qadariyya.

And His saying: ﴿and when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an﴾, it is His saying: "There is no god but Allah."

And His saying: ﴿they turn their backs in aversion (nufuran)﴾, meaning: fleeing.

A similar verse is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when Allah alone is mentioned, the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter recoil﴾.

The commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 17, verse 47:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿We know best what they listen for when they listen to you﴾. The people of tafsir (exegesis) said: "bihi" (with it) is a supplementary particle (silah), and its meaning is: "We know best what they listen for," i.e., what they seek to hear. This is in the sense of His words: ﴿And when those who are other than Him are mentioned, behold, they rejoice﴾.

And His words: ﴿When they listen to you, and when they are in private consultation (najwa)﴾, meaning: those who hold a private consultation (dhu najwa). In the narration: the Prophet (ﷺ) was reciting, and the polytheists had gathered, and they would confer among themselves. One would say, "He is a soothsayer (kahin)"; another would say, "He is a sorcerer (sahir)"; another would say, "He is a poet (shá'ir)"; another would say, "He is possessed (majnun)"; and they meant by this the Messenger.

And His words: ﴿When the wrongdoers say, "You follow only a man bewitched (masuran)"﴾. Mujahid said: "deceived (makhdu'an)." Abu 'Ubayda said: "a man who has sihr, and sihr is the windpipe (ri'a)," meaning that he is a human being. The poet said:

(Arana mawdi'in (lahtum) ghayb... wa-nuhsaru bil-ta'ami wa-bil-sharab)
i.e., we are fed and deceived; and this is on the interpretation of deception, and it is the more correct view.

It was also said: "masuran" means turned away from the truth.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 48:

And His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Look how they coin for you the parables﴾, i.e., the likenesses (al-ashbah).

And His saying: ﴿So they have gone astray, and they cannot find a way﴾, i.e., they cannot reach a path to the truth.

Almighty Allah says: ﴿And they say, "When we have become bones and dust, shall we really be resurrected as a new creation?"﴾ Al-Farra' said: "Rufatan" means dust. Others said: "Rufatan" means crumbled fragments, i.e., when we have been broken into pieces.

As for His words, ﴿Shall we really be resurrected as a new creation?﴾, they said this by way of denial (inkar).

"The saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Say: Be you stones or iron﴾. If it is asked: How can He command them to become stones or iron, when they are certainly unable to do so? The answer: This is a command of incapacitation (ta'jiz), and it is not a command of obligation (ilzam). The meaning of the verse is: Feel in your hearts that you are stones or iron; for if you were such, you would not escape Me. It has also been said that its meaning is: If you had been created from stones and iron instead of flesh and bone, you would still die and then be resurrected. This was said by Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 51:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or a creation of what is greater in your breasts﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, and 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As said: it is death. Its meaning: even if you were death itself, death would overtake you.

It has been established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Death will be brought on the Day of Resurrection in the form of a dusty ram. It will be stopped between Paradise and Hell; all of them will recognise it, and it will be slaughtered. Then it will be said: O people of Paradise, eternity for you and no death! And O people of Hell, eternity and no death!"

It is related from Mujahid that the meaning of His saying: ﴿Or a creation of what is greater in your breasts﴾ is the heavens, the earth, and the mountains. That is: if you were such, you would indeed die and be resurrected.

Qatadah said: it is everything that is great in the eye and breast of a human being. It is related from al-Kalbi that he said: it is the Resurrection.

As for His saying: ﴿So they will say, "Who will restore us?"﴾, its meaning is clear.

As for His saying: ﴿Say, "He who created you the first time."﴾ That is: He who brought you into being the first time. And whoever is able to originate is more able to restore.

As for His saying: ﴿So they will shake their heads at you﴾ That is: they will move their heads toward you, and this is in the manner of mockery.

As for His saying: ﴿And they say, "When will it be?"﴾ That is: when is the Hour? They also said this in mockery.

As for His saying: ﴿Say, "It may be that it is near."﴾ Its meaning: it is near. And "perhaps" (ʿasā) from God is binding, as we have explained.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 52:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the Day He calls you, and you respond with His praise﴾, meaning: praising Him. If it is said: How can this be valid, when the address is to the disbelievers, and how can a disbeliever be raised praising his Lord?

The answer has two aspects. The first: the address is to the believers, and the address to the disbelievers ends at this verse.

The second view: the address is to the disbelievers, and the meaning of His saying ﴿and you respond with His praise﴾ is: acknowledging that He is your Creator and the One who raises you.

As for His saying ﴿and you will think that you had not remained but a little﴾, this is in comparison with the duration of the Resurrection (and the eternity). So if a person remained in his grave for thousands of years, that would be counted as little in comparison with the eternity he will reach.

It is related from Qatadah, who said: They will regard the duration of the world as trivial in comparison with the Resurrection.

It is related from Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah, who said: They will stand and say: "Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You."  The more appropriate view is that this applies to the believers.

Al-Kalbi said: Allah, exalted is He, lifts the punishment from the disbelievers between the two blasts, which is forty years. So when they are raised, having rested during that period, they say: "We remained only a little."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 53:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And say to My servants that they should speak that which is best﴾. Regarding this verse there are two opinions. The more widespread and the more apparent is that His saying ﴿they should speak that which is best﴾ refers to the disbelievers, and this was before the revelation of the verse of the sword.

The people of tafsir said: The polytheists used to harm the believers, and the believers would seek the permission of the Messenger of Allah to fight, and he would forbid them from that and command them to speak in the best manner. Speaking in the best manner is their saying to the disbelievers: "May Allah guide you." It is also reported in some narrations that ʿUmar was insulted by some of the disbelievers, so he wanted to fight him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded him to overlook and pardon.

The second opinion regarding the verse is that what is meant by it is the believers, and the meaning is that they should say and do that which is best, i.e., the characteristic which is best.

It has also been said that what is meant by it is the enjoining of what is good and the forbidding of what is evil.

As for His saying, ﴿Indeed, Satan incites discord among them﴾, i.e., he corrupts by provoking enmity. And His saying, ﴿Indeed, Satan is ever to mankind a clear enemy﴾, i.e., an enemy whose enmity is evident.

The exegesis of His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Your Lord knows you best. If He wills, He will have mercy upon you, or if He wills, He will punish you.﴾ He said: "He will have mercy upon you" through guidance and direction, and "He will punish you" through misguidance. It was also said: "He will have mercy upon you" by rescuing you from the Fire, or "He will punish you" by casting you into it.

As for His words: ﴿And We have not sent you over them as a guardian.﴾ That is, as a guarantor (kafil). The poet said:

("You reminded me of Abu Arwa, so I spent the night as if I were... the one who manages (barada) the past affairs as a guardian (wakil)"). That is, a guarantor (kafil).

Among them are those who said its meaning is: He did not empower you over them by preventing them from disbelief.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 55:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And your Lord knows best who is in the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning: your Lord, who knows those in the heavens and the earth, and He is the One who knows their states, their actions, and their intentions.
